terms.grammar: noun, third declension: with the genitive of the thing or a gerund (cupiditās videndī)
evidence: Cic. Att. 12.26.1: vel studiō potius et cupiditāte nōn dubitō
terms.comment: The general word for wanting something strongly, in a good sense (cupiditās vērī videndī, Cic. Tusc. 1.44) and, more often, a bad one: greed, ambition, lust (Lewis & Short). The verb is cupiō (see want).

terms.gloss: longing for something absent or lost
terms.grammar: noun, second declension: with the genitive
evidence: Cic. Att. 5.11.1: nōn dīcī potest quam flagrem dēsīderiō urbis
terms.comment: Desire for what one has had and misses: a person, home, a place (see homesickness, I miss you). Its verb is dēsīderāre, to long for, to miss.

terms.register: vōx plērumque historicōrum et poētārum: Sall., Liv., Verg.
evidence: Liv. 1.6.3: Rōmulum Remumque cupīdō cēpit … urbis condendae
terms.comment: The historians’ word, often in the phrase cupīdō cēpit, “the desire took him”; masculine in the poets. Cicero uses it only of the god Cupid (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Rōmulum Remumque cupīdō cēpit in iīs locīs ubi expositī ubique ēducātī erant urbis condendae
phrases.english: Romulus and Remus were seized by the desire to found a city in the place where they had been left and brought up

phrases.latin: adeō quantō rērum minus, tantō minus cupiditātis erat
phrases.english: the less people had, the less they wanted

phrases.latin: nōn dīcī potest quam flagrem dēsīderiō urbis
phrases.english: words can’t say how I burn with longing for Rome
